body.text: On October 23, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that Confucius Institutes – overseas language and cultural programs funded and run by the Chinese government globally – would be designated as a national security threat, adding that the department had shut down 80 such “propaganda cells” appearing under different names across 30 universities. While Hegseth did not specify which entities were implicated, the Pentagon had announced just a few days earlier the results of research security audits of 30 universities that terminated over 80 partnerships, including with foreign entities on the NDAA Section 1286 blacklist.

China’s evolving and large-scale efforts to gain a strategic foothold in universities – reshaping discourse, repressing freedom of speech, controlling Chinese students, and leveraging technology and talent – require concerted yet targeted responses that establish needed safeguards while preserving the innovative spirit of U.S. higher education.

Confucius Institutes are indeed a cause for concern because they provide a direct propaganda vehicle for the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to promote a one-sided view of China and its policies while pressuring the censorship of politically sensitive topics. Campuses nationwide saw a wave of CI closures after the U.S. government in 2018 barred universities hosting such institutes from receiving Pentagon funding. But subsequent reports found that several universities had simply continued similar partnerships under different names, while new nonprofits run by CI-linked personnel emerged to run educational programming, including in K-12 schools.

Rebranding is a classic tactic from the Chinese government’s playbook. When the Made in China 2025 initiative, an expansive roadmap to transform the country into a global high-tech leader, sparked alarm in Western capitals, Beijing quietly retired the name while continuing the same large-scale industrial policies that has enabled it to dominate advanced manufacturing in many strategic sectors. Similarly, the well-known Thousand Talents Plan to attract overseas scientists to China with expansive funding and resources has been subsumed by multiple national and subnational talent recruitment programs. Confucius Institutes by any other name will still imbue the CCP’s goals of reclaiming global “discourse power” and using the guise of education to spread pro-China narratives.

It’s unclear how much CIs have shifted attitudes to favor China. But such educational initiatives are just one of myriad ways in which Beijing tries to exploit the openness of U.S. higher-ed institutions. Beyond propaganda messaging and threats to academic freedom, the Chinese Communist Party has sought to extend its long arm of surveillance and repression into university campuses. It has called on Chinese students overseas to further CCP influence efforts and “tell China’s story well.” Chinese Students and Scholars Associations (CSSAs) have disrupted events featuring critics of the CCP and denounced dissident art as racist. While most Chinese students are not intending to be a part of the CCP’s machinery, they can be vulnerable to coercion and incentivized to mobilize by Beijing. This creates a chilling environment on campuses where students and faculty must constantly look over their shoulders.

Financial incentives, whether from foreign student tuition or foreign and private grants, leave universities poorly placed to self-police foreign malign influence attempts. Confucius Institutes were able to reappear in various forms because of willing U.S. counterparts in university administrators. This does not mean that universities should compromise their independence or that government should legislate academic freedoms. But toughened enforcement of penalties on institutions and researchers for failing to disclose foreign collaborations and funding has signaled the importance of transparency and accountability.

Standardizing disclosure requirements and the lists of off-limit foreign entities – presently an inconsistent patchwork across different federal funding agencies – would reduce loopholes and provide a more navigable landscape for higher ed institutions. Policymakers should also mandate that universities implement a reporting framework for transnational repression incidents occurring on campus or involving students, faculty, and staff. This would empower victims and consolidate institutional memory of malign influence attempts.

Academic exchanges and collaborations are important aspects of higher education and scientific research. Openness has allowed U.S. universities to become engines of innovation and economic growth that attract students and research talent from around the world. But China does not respect an equal playing field. Because the Chinese government has politicized and will politicize relationships for its own economic and strategic gain, we need to enact appropriate guardrails while avoiding overly sweeping policies.
